qt: to the Commission Eva Kaili (NI) Subject:

Sustainable Development Goal 7 aims to ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all1. The human right to energy access is not yet fully enshrined in the EU’s legal framework. According to EU law, energy rights are categorised under consumer protection and include the right to choose a supplier, switch supplier when necessary and have access to electricity2. Regarding this, in order to address the practice of multinationals segmenting the single market into geographically isolated smaller markets by introducing barriers to competition, parallel imports and the arbitrage of retailers: 1.

What current comparative data does the Commission have on the measures adopted by each Member State to protect the right to energy access and combat energy poverty such as minimum energy allowances and the promotion of energy efficiency in low-income homes?

When will an EU observatory that tracks real time energy prices by Member State become available in order to protect citizens from the asymmetric power of large multinational companies that apply different pricing policies to individual Member States?
What legislation is being proposed to effectively address the practice of territorial supply constraints, when they are not justified by objective factors that promote the well-being of our society?
at: (English version) to the Commission Eva Kaili (NI) (15 March 2024) Subject: Energy poverty and the right to energy access in the European Union Sustainable Development Goal 7 aims to ensure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all (1). The human right to energy access is not yet fully enshrined in the EU’s legal framework. According to EU law, energy rights are categorised under consumer protection and include the right to choose a supplier, switch supplier when necessary and have access to electricity (2). Regarding this, in order to address the practice of multinationals segmenting the single market into geographically isolated smaller markets by introducing barriers to competition, parallel imports and the arbitrage of retailers: 1.

(12 August 2024) With the Fit for 55 Package and REPower EU initiatives, the European Union has adopted a strengthened framework for consumer protection, information, and empowerment in the EU (1). This accelerated actions to alleviate energy poverty. The Energy Efficiency Directive (EED) provides for the first time an EUwide definition of energy poverty. The new legislative framework ensures the right to energy access, sets new standards for transparency regarding contractual terms and conditions, provides the right to easily switch to a new supplier and it fully protects energy poor and vulnerable consumers, for example, from electricity disconnections. The provisions on the National Energy and Climate Plans (2) require Member States to report the number of energy poor households and to set out policies to address this serious situation. In addition, the EED recast (3) and the Energy Performance of Building Directive (EPBD) recast (4) establish energy efficiency measures as one of the most effective ways to address energy poverty and require Member States to set targets for energy efficiency actions for low-income households, particularly building renovations. The continued roll out of smart meters in Member States gives consumers objective and transparent near-real time metering data about their consumption and empowers them through digitalisation to be more active in the energy transition (5).
